"Say 'water' again, Noor. Wah-tar!" Jiten's voice carried down the corridor, and two boys laughed.
Noor's ears burned. "My name is Noor, and it's not funny."
"Relax, it's a joke."
Thomas looked up from the steps, where he was eating his lunch. "It didn't sound like one."
Later, by the water tank, Noor said quietly, "Part of me wants to talk flat, like everyone else."
"Why would you? I like how you say things," said Thomas. "If he keeps doing it, tell Mrs. Bhatt. And sit with us tomorrow, we keep the corner bench." 🙂
Noor nodded slowly. "Okay. If it happens again, I'll tell her on Monday."

qa.q: Which word did Jiten ask Noor to say again?
qa.a: He asked Noor to say 'water' again, mocking the way Noor pronounces it.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling by the water tank, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Noor felt hurt and self-conscious: the burning ears and the wish to talk flat, like everyone else, show the teasing stung.

qa.q: What could Noor do if the teasing keeps going?
qa.a: Noor could tell Mrs. Bhatt, as planned, and keep sitting on the corner bench with people who like how Noor talks. There is no need to change the accent.

qa.q: How might Thomas have seen the moment in the corridor?
qa.a: Thomas thought the remark did not sound like a joke and saw that Noor was hurt, so Thomas offered a seat on the bench and some backup. 🙂

grounding: A classmate teases Noor for the way Noor speaks; Noor is encouraged to keep the accent, tell a teacher if it continues, and sit with people who value Noor.

Lucia stood at the door of the art room with her portfolio pressed to her chest, ready to be told the club was full. She had moved to the town in September, spoke slowly in the new language, and had eaten lunch alone for three weeks.
Ms. Esther glanced up from sorting brushes. "You must be Lucia. There's a stool by the window, and the kettle is on if you want tea."
Nobody asked where she was from or why she talked that way. Lucia sat down, and her shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks. When the bell rang she stayed to wash the brushes.
"Same time Thursday?" Ms. Esther said.
Lucia nodded. Walking out, she decided that next month she would save a stool for whoever came in next.

qa.q: Where did Lucia sit in the art room?
qa.a: She sat on the stool by the window.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when her shoulders dropped?
qa.a: She felt relief: she had expected to be turned away, and the easy welcome without questions let her relax at last. 😊

qa.q: How could Lucia hold on to this kindness?
qa.a: She can keep the Thursday club as an anchor, and later, as she plans, save a stool for the next newcomer.

qa.q: How might Ms. Esther see what happened at the door?
qa.a: To Ms. Esther it may have been an ordinary welcome to a new student, though it meant far more to Lucia after weeks of eating alone.

grounding: A teacher welcomes a newcomer without judgment, she feels deep relief, and she resolves to pay the kindness forward.

"Sit, Naveen. Your Farhan uncle wasn't always this quiet. When I was fifteen, our class went on an exchange trip to Chennai, and I was proud, beta, of my Urdu, my mother's biryani, the couplets we recite at Eid.
A boy called Murali asked what a ghazal was, so I recited one, chest out. Then he sang a Tamil song his grandmother sang, and I caught myself wanting to know every word.
I nearly said 'ours is better.' But I saw how his eyes lit up. So I asked him to teach me the chorus, and he asked me to teach him the couplet.
By the last night we were singing both on the dorm roof. My pride never shrank, Naveen. It just made room."

qa.q: What did Farhan recite for Murali on the trip?
qa.a: He recited a ghazal, a couplet in Urdu, after Murali asked what a ghazal was.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he nearly said 'ours is better', and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He was swelling with pride in his language and culture, but seeing Murali's eyes light up made him curious instead.

qa.q: How can someone be proud of where they come from without putting others down?
qa.a: Like Farhan, they can share their own songs and ask to learn the other person's, so pride and curiosity sit side by side.

qa.q: How might Murali have felt when Farhan asked him to teach the chorus?
qa.a: Murali probably felt pleased and respected, since he answered by asking Farhan to teach him the couplet in return.

grounding: An elder recalls teenage pride in his language and culture, held alongside curiosity about another boy's, without putting anyone down.

Monday. Sumit noticed that Urmila left before the last bell every day. He guessed she was skipping class, and he almost said so to his bench mate.
Wednesday. Instead he asked her, "I've seen you rush out. Do you mind telling me where you go?"
Urmila laughed. "Tiffin delivery. Mum's kitchen sends out forty boxes, and I do the last route by bicycle."
He listened while she described the office towers, the regulars, the security guard who always waits with a joke. "Sorry I assumed," he said.
The next Tuesday, Sumit brought a bag of questions, and one of his own tiffin boxes to swap. "Teach me how you fold the rotis so they stay soft," he said, and Urmila showed him.

qa.q: What does Urmila do after school?
qa.a: She does the last route of her mum's tiffin delivery by bicycle.

qa.q: Why did Sumit stop himself from repeating his guess to his bench mate?
qa.a: He realised he did not really know why Urmila left early, and he chose to ask her respectfully instead of assuming.

qa.q: What could Sumit do next to keep learning from Urmila?
qa.a: He could keep asking open questions and listening more than guessing, and perhaps join a delivery route one weekend if Urmila invites him. 🙂

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt about being asked rather than judged?
qa.a: She probably felt respected: she laughed, explained freely and showed him how to fold the rotis, which suggests the question felt friendly.

grounding: Sumit meets a classmate whose life is very different, asks respectfully, listens instead of assuming, and learns from the difference.

Class teacher's note, Tuesday. Chandrika stayed back after the last bell, her jaw tight. She told me a classmate had said her family "lives on charity" and that people from her village don't belong at this school. She felt small, she said, and wanted to shout, but she said nothing.
I told her the remark shows the classmate's bias and says nothing about her family. I asked what she wanted me to do. She asked me to speak to the class without naming her.
I did that on Wednesday morning, in a lesson on respect. At lunch I saw Chandrika at the corner bench with Amandeep and two others, laughing. I will check in with her on Friday and will speak with the classmate separately.
Mrs. Verma

qa.q: What did the classmate say about Chandrika's family?
qa.a: The classmate said her family "lives on charity".

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she stayed back after the bell?
qa.a: She felt small and angry: her tight jaw and her wish to shout, even though she said nothing, show it.

qa.q: What would you advise Chandrika if the remarks start again?
qa.a: She can tell Mrs. Verma again, remember that the remark reflects the classmate's bias and not her worth, and stay close to Amandeep and the friends who respect her.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Verma have seen Chandrika's request not to be named?
qa.a: Mrs. Verma likely saw it as a way to protect Chandrika from extra attention, so she raised respect with the whole class instead.

grounding: A classmate's remarks about family income and village leave Chandrika small and angry; the teacher frames it as the classmate's bias and she stays with respectful friends.

Counsellor's note, Thursday. Hemant, Class 10, asked to see me in his free period. He was angry and said so: the library shuts at 3:30 for students who take the colony bus, while day scholars from town may stay until 5.
He had not shouted at the librarian. Instead he had kept a page for three weeks with dates, times and who was sent out. Omkar, a day scholar, had signed under it to say he had seen it happen.
I told Hemant his anger was fair, and that a written page would carry further than a raised voice. We drafted a short request asking the principal to review the rule, and he chose to hand it in himself.
The rule was made for bus timings, and I doubt anyone had noticed its effect. I will ask for a reply by next week.
Mr. Rane

qa.q: For how many weeks had Hemant kept his page of dates and times?
qa.a: He had kept it for three weeks.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was angry: he said so, and he spent three weeks recording each incident instead of letting it pass.

qa.q: What could Hemant do if the principal does not reply?
qa.a: He could ask Mr. Rane and his allies such as Omkar for help in taking the facts to the next formal complaint route.

qa.q: Why might the principal have made the rule without noticing its effect?
qa.a: The rule was made for bus timings, so the principal may not have seen that it sent the colony students out of the library while day scholars could stay.

grounding: A school rule treats students who take the colony bus unfairly; Hemant documents facts, gets an ally's signature and uses the formal request route.

passage:
"Charu, can I tell you something embarrassing?"
"Go on."
"When you invited me over, I expected your house to be dirty. Ammamma always says people from your street don't care about cleanliness."
Charu raised an eyebrow. "And?"
"Your kitchen was cleaner than mine. I felt stupid. I've heard that line since I was small and never checked it."
"Thanks for saying it," said Charu. "Most people just think it."
"I'm not going to beat myself up," Rekha said. "I'll just notice when the thought pops up and check it against real people. Can I come again on Sunday?"
"Bring your notes. We can study together."

qa.q: What does Rekha's Ammamma always say about Charu's street?
qa.a: She always says people from Charu's street don't care about cleanliness.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she saw Charu's kitchen?
qa.a: She felt stupid and embarrassed, because what she saw contradicted the line she had heard since she was small.

qa.q: What is Rekha planning to do about her stereotypes?
qa.a: She will notice when the thought pops up and check it against real people, without beating herself up.

qa.q: How might Charu have seen Rekha's confession?
qa.a: Charu seems to value the honesty, saying most people just think it, and offers to study together on Sunday.

grounding: Rekha notices a stereotype absorbed at home about Charu's community, names it, meets the real person and chooses to unlearn it without self-hate.

passage:
In the chemistry lab, Dilnaz was rinsing a pipette when a boy at the next bench said to Maria, "Go back to where you came from." A few others snorted.
Dilnaz froze. Her heart thumped, and while she searched for words the moment passed. Maria packed her bag in silence. Mr. Fernandes was at the far end of the room, writing on the board.
In the corridor Dilnaz caught up with her. "I should have said something. That wasn't okay. Are you alright?"
"I wasn't sure anyone had heard," Maria said.
"I heard. Do you want to sit together at lunch? And if you decide to tell Mr. Fernandes, I'll say what I heard."
Maria let out a slow breath. "Maybe. Lunch first."

qa.q: Where did the remark happen?
qa.a: It happened in the chemistry lab, at the bench next to Dilnaz's.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz freeze instead of speaking up?
qa.a: She was caught off guard: her heart thumped and she was still searching for words when the moment passed.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do if she hears a remark like that again?
qa.a: She could say plainly 'that isn't okay' right away, and keep checking on Maria afterwards, as she did in the corridor.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when nobody spoke in the lab?
qa.a: Maria may have felt alone and unsure anyone had heard, which is why she said so, and why Dilnaz's check-in mattered to her.

grounding: A friend hesitates at a bigoted remark aimed at Maria, then makes a small stand afterwards by checking on her and offering to back her up.

passage:
Okay, so, I'm Yusuf, and this one still bothers me. At my cousin's engagement dinner I mentioned that my friend Abhinav would come by to help with the tent. My Chachi put down her spoon and said, "Those people keep different habits. Be careful who you bring in." Two aunts nodded.
My face went hot. I said, "Chachi, Abhinav is my friend, and I didn't like how that sounded." Nobody answered. Later Dadi told me I had been disrespectful.
Maybe I was a bit sharp. But I wasn't going to sit silent. Abhinav came on Saturday anyway and carried poles all afternoon, and Chachi handed him a glass of water.
It's not fixed. I know elders don't change overnight. But I'm not dropping my friend.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do at the engagement on Saturday?
qa.a: He carried poles all afternoon and helped with the tent.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when the aunts nodded, and what did he decide?
qa.a: His face went hot, which suggests discomfort and anger, and he decided to disagree respectfully without giving up his friend.

qa.q: How could Yusuf handle relatives who look down on his friend over time?
qa.a: He can keep disagreeing politely when it comes up and keep the friendship, being patient because elders change slowly, and small moments like the glass of water may help.

qa.q: How might Dadi have seen what Yusuf said to Chachi?
qa.a: Dadi saw it as disrespect toward an elder, so she probably cared more about how he spoke than about what he was defending.

grounding: Yusuf's relatives look down on his friend from another community; he respectfully disagrees, keeps the friend and accepts that elders change slowly.

passage:
On his second Monday at the new school in Bengaluru, Asif opened his tiffin and the smell of sheermal and korma drifted across the room. Two boys wrinkled their noses. "What is that? Sooo spicy," one said, and the other copied the way Asif said "aap" until the bench laughed.
Asif closed the lid halfway and answered every question in one word. That evening he told his mother he wanted plain bread from tomorrow.
Karthik, at the next bench, had heard it all. "Can I try a piece?" he asked the next day, and afterwards handed over an idli. "Tell me how to say sheermal properly. I'll teach you some Kannada."
Asif packed the korma again.

qa.q: What was in Asif's tiffin?
qa.a: There was sheermal and korma.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling in his first weeks, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt homesick and self-conscious: he closed the lid halfway, gave one-word answers and asked his mother for plain bread.

qa.q: What could Asif do to settle in without losing himself?
qa.a: He can keep bringing food from home and speaking his own way, learn some Kannada slowly with Karthik, and keep the one or two allies close.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Asif's food?
qa.a: Karthik sees it as something to be curious about: he asks to try it and offers an idli in exchange, rather than wrinkling his nose.

grounding: A boy who moved to a new city is teased for his language and food, keeps his roots and finds an ally who trades words and food.
